questions.title: Running balance and overdraft flag
questions.scenario: The branch operations head wants a passbook-style statement. For every transaction she needs the balance after it, and a flag wherever the account went below zero.
questions.schema:
TXN(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_ts DATE, dr_cr CHAR(2), amount NUMBER(14,2))
-- dr_cr is 'CR' or 'DR'; assume opening balance 0
questions.task: Show acct_id, txn_id, txn_ts, running balance, and OVERDRAFT = 'Y' when the running balance is negative.
questions.hint: SUM() OVER with a signed amount; order by time and txn_id so ties are stable.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id, txn_id, txn_ts, bal,
       CASE WHEN bal < 0 THEN 'Y' ELSE 'N' END AS overdraft
FROM (
  SELECT t.*,
         SUM(CASE dr_cr WHEN 'CR' THEN amount ELSE -amount END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY acct_id
                 ORDER BY txn_ts, txn_id
                 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS bal
  FROM txn t
);
questions.why: The window sums signed amounts from the first row up to the current row per account. ROWS (not the default RANGE) plus txn_id in the ORDER BY stops two transactions with the same timestamp from sharing one balance.
questions.tip: I always add a tiebreaker to ORDER BY and state ROWS explicitly, because the default RANGE frame gives wrong balances when timestamps tie.
questions.simple: Think of your bank passbook. After every entry there is a balance column. To get that number you add up every deposit and subtract every withdrawal from the first line down to this line. SUM() OVER does exactly that adding for each row. If two entries happen at the same second, you also sort by txn_id so each entry still gets its own balance.
questions.remember: Running balance = keep adding from the top, row by row (ROWS).

questions.title: Three EMIs missed in a row
questions.scenario: Credit risk wants an early-warning list: loans where the customer missed 3 or more consecutive monthly EMIs. One-off misses should not appear.
questions.schema:
EMI_SCHEDULE(loan_id NUMBER, due_month DATE, status VARCHAR2(10))
-- due_month is the 1st of each month; status is 'PAID' or 'MISSED'
questions.task: Return loan_id, first missed month, last missed month and the streak length for every streak of 3+ consecutive MISSED months.
questions.hint: Consecutive months minus a row number give a constant value for each streak.
questions.solution:
SELECT loan_id, MIN(due_month) AS first_missed,
       MAX(due_month) AS last_missed, COUNT(*) AS streak
FROM (
  SELECT loan_id, due_month,
         ADD_MONTHS(due_month,
           -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY loan_id ORDER BY due_month)) AS grp
  FROM emi_schedule
  WHERE status = 'MISSED'
)
GROUP BY loan_id, grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
questions.why: Within one unbroken streak, each month moves forward by one and so does the row number, so month minus row number stays constant. A gap changes that value and starts a new group.
questions.tip: This is the gaps-and-islands pattern; I use it for consecutive defaults, login streaks and missing sequence numbers.
questions.simple: Imagine ticking a calendar for each month the EMI was missed. You want to find 3 or more ticks next to each other with no gap. A trick: number the missed months 1, 2, 3... and subtract that number from the month. If the months are back to back, the answer stays the same, so they fall in one group. A gap changes the answer and starts a new group.
questions.remember: Month minus counter stays the same while the streak lasts.

questions.title: Card velocity check
questions.scenario: The fraud team suspects card testing. They want every card transaction that is the 3rd or later swipe on the same card within any 10-minute window.
questions.schema: CARD_TXN(txn_id NUMBER, card_no VARCHAR2(19), txn_ts DATE, merchant_id NUMBER, amount NUMBER(12,2))
questions.task: List txn_id, card_no, txn_ts and the count of transactions on that card in the 10 minutes up to and including this one, where the count is 3 or more.
questions.hint: A RANGE frame can look back by a time interval instead of a number of rows.
questions.solution:
SELECT txn_id, card_no, txn_ts, cnt_10m
FROM (
  SELECT c.*,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY card_no
                        ORDER BY txn_ts
                        RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING
                                  AND CURRENT ROW) AS cnt_10m
  FROM card_txn c
)
WHERE cnt_10m >= 3;
questions.why: RANGE works on the ORDER BY value, so the frame holds every row whose timestamp is within the last 10 minutes, however many rows that is. ROWS could not express a time window.
questions.tip: ROWS counts physical rows, RANGE works on values; for time-based velocity rules I use RANGE with an INTERVAL.
questions.simple: Picture a 10-minute stopwatch that moves along with every swipe of a card. At each swipe you look back 10 minutes and count how many swipes you see. If you count 3 or more, it looks like someone is testing a stolen card. RANGE with INTERVAL '10' MINUTE is that stopwatch.
questions.remember: RANGE looks back by time, ROWS looks back by count.

questions.title: Top 3 depositors per branch
questions.scenario: Each branch manager must call their top 3 depositors before the quarter closes. If customers tie on balance, all of them must be on the list.
questions.schema:
ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, branch_id NUMBER, balance NUMBER(16,2), status VARCHAR2(10))
-- one customer can hold several accounts in a branch
questions.task: For each branch show the customers whose total balance across ACTIVE accounts is in the top 3 distinct totals, with their rank.
questions.hint: Aggregate per customer first, then rank. Think about which ranking function keeps ties.
questions.solution:
SELECT branch_id, cust_id, total_bal, rnk
FROM (
  SELECT branch_id, cust_id, SUM(balance) AS total_bal,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id
                            ORDER BY SUM(balance) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM account
  WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
  GROUP BY branch_id, cust_id
)
WHERE rnk <= 3;
questions.why: Analytic functions run after GROUP BY, so you can rank on SUM(balance) directly. DENSE_RANK keeps tied customers and leaves no gaps, so rank 3 always exists when there are 3 distinct totals.
questions.tip: ROW_NUMBER drops ties, RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK does neither; I pick based on what the business means by top 3.
questions.simple: It is like a race where two runners finish at the same time. Both get a medal. First you add up each customer's money across all their accounts. Then you give ranks inside each branch. DENSE_RANK lets people who tie share the same rank, and the next rank is not skipped, so you never lose a 3rd place.
questions.remember: Ties share a rank: DENSE_RANK. No ties allowed: ROW_NUMBER.

questions.title: Duplicate UPI postings
questions.scenario: A retry bug posted some UPI transactions twice with the same UTR number. Finance wants the duplicates removed before settlement, keeping the earliest posting of each UTR.
questions.schema:
UPI_TXN(id NUMBER, utr_no VARCHAR2(22), payer_vpa VARCHAR2(50), payee_vpa VARCHAR2(50),
        amount NUMBER(12,2), created_ts TIMESTAMP)
questions.task: Write a single DELETE that removes every duplicate row and keeps the earliest row per utr_no.
questions.hint: Number the rows inside each UTR and delete by ROWID.
questions.solution:
DELETE FROM upi_txn
WHERE rowid IN (
  SELECT rid
  FROM (
    SELECT rowid AS rid,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY utr_no
                              ORDER BY created_ts, id) AS rn
    FROM upi_txn
  )
  WHERE rn > 1
);
questions.why: ROW_NUMBER gives 1 to the row you keep and 2, 3... to the copies. Deleting by ROWID is the fastest way to hit the exact physical rows.
questions.tip: Before deleting in production I run the inner query as a SELECT, save the rows to a backup table, and then add a unique constraint on the UTR so it cannot happen again.
questions.simple: Imagine the same payment slip was photocopied by mistake. You keep the first copy and throw away the rest. ROW_NUMBER gives the first copy number 1 and the copies 2, 3 and so on. Then you delete everything that is not number 1.
questions.remember: Number the copies, keep number 1, delete the rest.

questions.title: Apply staged transactions to balances
questions.scenario: The end-of-day job loads the day's transactions into a staging table. Balances must be updated for existing accounts, and a balance row created for accounts seen for the first time.
questions.schema:
STG_TXN(acct_id NUMBER, amount NUMBER(14,2))        -- signed: credits positive, debits negative
ACCT_BALANCE(acct_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, balance NUMBER(16,2), updated_on DATE)
questions.task: Write one statement that adds each account's net staged amount to its balance, inserting a row when the account is not yet in ACCT_BALANCE.
questions.hint: Aggregate the staging table inside the USING clause so each account appears once.
questions.solution:
MERGE INTO acct_balance t
USING (SELECT acct_id, SUM(amount) AS net
       FROM stg_txn
       GROUP BY acct_id) s
ON (t.acct_id = s.acct_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET t.balance = t.balance + s.net,
             t.updated_on = SYSDATE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (acct_id, balance, updated_on)
  VALUES (s.acct_id, s.net, SYSDATE);
questions.why: MERGE does the update and the insert in one pass. Aggregating in USING matters: if the source has two rows for one account, Oracle raises ORA-30926 (unable to get a stable set of rows).
questions.tip: I make the MERGE source unique on the join key, otherwise ORA-30926 appears in production the first day an account has two staged rows.
questions.simple: Think of a class attendance register. If a student's name is already in the register, you update their marks. If it is a new student, you add a new line. MERGE does both in one go. First add up each account's money for the day, so each account comes only once.
questions.remember: MERGE = update if it exists, insert if it is new.

questions.title: Core banking versus general ledger
questions.scenario: At month-end, finance reconciles branch totals from core banking against the general ledger. They need only the problems: branches missing on either side, or where the amounts differ.
questions.schema:
CBS_TOTAL(branch_id NUMBER, total_amt NUMBER(18,2))
GL_TOTAL (branch_id NUMBER, total_amt NUMBER(18,2))
questions.task: Return branch_id, CBS amount, GL amount, difference, and a status of 'MISSING IN GL', 'MISSING IN CBS' or 'AMOUNT MISMATCH'. Matching branches must not appear.
questions.hint: A full outer join keeps rows from both sides; NULLs tell you which side is missing.
questions.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(c.branch_id, g.branch_id) AS branch_id,
       c.total_amt AS cbs_amt, g.total_amt AS gl_amt,
       NVL(c.total_amt, 0) - NVL(g.total_amt, 0) AS diff,
       CASE
         WHEN g.branch_id IS NULL THEN 'MISSING IN GL'
         WHEN c.branch_id IS NULL THEN 'MISSING IN CBS'
         ELSE 'AMOUNT MISMATCH'
       END AS status
FROM cbs_total c
FULL OUTER JOIN gl_total g ON g.branch_id = c.branch_id
WHERE c.branch_id IS NULL
   OR g.branch_id IS NULL
   OR c.total_amt <> g.total_amt;
questions.why: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched rows plus unmatched rows from each side. The WHERE keeps only breaks. Check the key columns for NULL, not the amounts, because an amount could itself be NULL.
questions.tip: This is the same source-versus-target pattern I used in data migration: count check, key check, then value check.
questions.simple: You and a friend each made a list of how much money each branch has. Now you lay both lists side by side. Some branches are only on your list, some only on your friend's list, and some are on both but with different numbers. A FULL OUTER JOIN puts both lists side by side so you can spot all three problems.
questions.remember: FULL OUTER JOIN = show rows from both lists, matched or not.

questions.title: Month-on-month AUM change
questions.scenario: The product team tracks assets under management per fund. They want each month's AUM next to the previous month's, with the percentage change.
questions.schema:
FUND_AUM(fund_id NUMBER, month_end DATE, aum NUMBER(18,2))
-- one row per fund per month
questions.task: Show fund_id, month_end, aum, previous month's aum and percentage change rounded to 2 decimals. The first month of each fund should show NULL change.
questions.hint: LAG reads the previous row in the partition. Guard against dividing by zero.
questions.solution:
SELECT fund_id, month_end, aum, prev_aum,
       ROUND((aum - prev_aum) / NULLIF(prev_aum, 0) * 100, 2) AS pct_change
FROM (
  SELECT f.*,
         LAG(aum) OVER (PARTITION BY fund_id ORDER BY month_end) AS prev_aum
  FROM fund_aum f
);
questions.why: LAG returns NULL for the first row, and any arithmetic with NULL stays NULL, which gives the required empty first month. NULLIF turns a zero denominator into NULL instead of raising ORA-01476.
questions.tip: LAG and LEAD replace a self-join, so the table is read once; that matters on large fact tables.
questions.simple: Think of your school report card. Next to this year's marks you write last year's marks and see if you went up or down. LAG brings last month's number onto this month's row so you can compare. The first month has nothing before it, so it stays empty.
questions.remember: LAG = peek at the row before me.

questions.title: Loan approval chain
questions.scenario: Audit wants to see the full approval chain for a loan officer: the officer, their manager, the manager's manager, up to the top.
questions.schema:
EMPLOYEE(emp_id NUMBER, emp_name VARCHAR2(60), mgr_id NUMBER, designation VARCHAR2(40))
-- mgr_id is NULL for the head
questions.task: For emp_id 4107, list each person in the chain upward with their level (1 = the officer) and the path of names from the officer to that person.
questions.hint: START WITH the officer and walk upward by connecting the parent's emp_id to the child's mgr_id.
questions.solution:
SELECT LEVEL AS lvl, emp_id, emp_name, designation,
       SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(emp_name, ' > ') AS chain
FROM employee
START WITH emp_id = 4107
CONNECT BY NOCYCLE PRIOR mgr_id = emp_id
ORDER BY LEVEL;
questions.why: PRIOR marks the row already visited. PRIOR mgr_id = emp_id means: the next row is the one whose emp_id equals my manager id, so the walk goes up. NOCYCLE protects against bad data where two people report to each other.
questions.tip: The side PRIOR sits on decides direction; I say it aloud as 'previous row's manager equals this row's id' to get it right.
questions.simple: Picture a family tree, but at work. You start with one officer and ask 'who is your boss?', then 'who is your boss's boss?', until you reach the top. CONNECT BY keeps climbing like this. PRIOR tells it which way to climb: up to the boss or down to the team.
questions.remember: START WITH me, CONNECT BY my boss, PRIOR shows the direction.

questions.title: Transaction count by channel per branch
questions.scenario: The digital banking head wants one row per branch with separate columns for UPI, NEFT, RTGS and IMPS transaction counts for the month.
questions.schema:
PAYMENT(pay_id NUMBER, branch_id NUMBER, channel VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(14,2), pay_date DATE)
-- channel is one of UPI, NEFT, RTGS, IMPS
questions.task: Produce branch_id with columns UPI, NEFT, RTGS, IMPS holding transaction counts for March 2026.
questions.hint: Select only the columns you need before PIVOT, otherwise extra columns become grouping columns.
questions.solution:
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT branch_id, channel
  FROM payment
  WHERE pay_date >= DATE '2026-03-01'
    AND pay_date <  DATE '2026-04-01'
)
PIVOT (COUNT(*) FOR channel IN ('UPI' AS upi, 'NEFT' AS neft,
                                'RTGS' AS rtgs, 'IMPS' AS imps))
ORDER BY branch_id;
questions.why: PIVOT groups by every column that is not in the aggregate or the FOR clause. The inline view leaves only branch_id, so you get one row per branch.
questions.tip: If the Oracle version or tool does not support PIVOT, I write the same thing with COUNT(CASE WHEN channel = 'UPI' THEN 1 END).
questions.simple: Imagine a long list that says 'Branch 1, UPI', 'Branch 1, NEFT', and so on. You want to turn it into a neat table with one row per branch and one column for each payment type. PIVOT turns those values into columns, like turning a list into a grid.
questions.remember: PIVOT turns row values into columns.

questions.title: Disbursals with subtotals
questions.scenario: The CFO's MIS report needs loan disbursal amounts by region and product, a subtotal for each region, and a grand total, all from one query.
questions.schema: LOAN(loan_id NUMBER, region VARCHAR2(20), product VARCHAR2(20), disbursed_amt NUMBER(16,2), disbursed_on DATE)
questions.task: Return region, product and total disbursed, with region subtotals labelled 'ALL PRODUCTS' and a final row labelled 'GRAND TOTAL'.
questions.hint: ROLLUP adds the subtotal rows; GROUPING() tells you which rows they are.
questions.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'GRAND TOTAL' ELSE region END AS region,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN NULL
            WHEN GROUPING(product) = 1 THEN 'ALL PRODUCTS'
            ELSE product END AS product,
       SUM(disbursed_amt) AS total_amt
FROM loan
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product)
ORDER BY GROUPING(region), region, GROUPING(product), product;
questions.why: ROLLUP(region, product) groups by (region, product), then (region), then (). GROUPING returns 1 on a subtotal row, which is safer than testing for NULL because the data itself may contain NULL products.
questions.tip: I use GROUPING() rather than NVL to label subtotals, since real NULLs in the column would otherwise be mislabelled as totals.
questions.simple: Think of a shopping bill. It lists each item, then a subtotal for each section, then a grand total at the bottom. ROLLUP adds those subtotal and grand total lines for you automatically. GROUPING() tells you which lines are totals so you can label them.
questions.remember: ROLLUP adds subtotals and a grand total.

questions.title: Latest KYC document per customer
questions.scenario: Compliance needs, for each customer, the date of their most recent KYC update and the document type used in that update.
questions.schema:
KYC_HISTORY(cust_id NUMBER, updated_on DATE, doc_type VARCHAR2(20), verified_by VARCHAR2(30))
-- many rows per customer
questions.task: Return one row per customer with the latest updated_on and the doc_type from that same row, without a subquery or self-join.
questions.hint: An aggregate can be told to look only at the rows ranked first or last by another column.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id,
       MAX(updated_on) AS last_kyc,
       MAX(doc_type) KEEP (DENSE_RANK LAST ORDER BY updated_on) AS last_doc
FROM kyc_history
GROUP BY cust_id;
questions.why: KEEP (DENSE_RANK LAST ORDER BY updated_on) restricts the aggregate to the rows with the latest date. MAX then just picks a value from those rows.
questions.tip: KEEP FIRST/LAST gets 'the value from the latest row' in one pass; the alternative is ROW_NUMBER in a subquery, which I use when I need many columns.
questions.simple: Imagine a pile of ID cards a customer showed over the years. You want the newest one and what type it was. KEEP DENSE_RANK LAST says: 'look only at the newest date, and take the document type from that row.'
questions.remember: KEEP LAST = take a value from the latest row.

questions.title: 7-day moving average price
questions.scenario: The equity desk wants a 7-day moving average of closing price per stock. For the first 6 days of a stock there is not enough data, so the average should be NULL.
questions.schema:
DAILY_PRICE(symbol VARCHAR2(12), trade_date DATE, close_price NUMBER(12,2))
-- one row per symbol per trading day
questions.task: Show symbol, trade_date, close_price and ma7 (average of this and the previous 6 trading days, 2 decimals), NULL until 7 rows exist.
questions.hint: Use a ROWS frame of 6 PRECEDING, and count the rows in the same frame.
questions.solution:
SELECT symbol, trade_date, close_price,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(*) OVER w = 7
            THEN ROUND(AVG(close_price) OVER w, 2) END AS ma7
FROM daily_price
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY trade_date
             ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW);
questions.why: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is a 7-row sliding frame. Counting rows in the same frame tells you when the frame is full. The WINDOW clause (19c patch sets and later) avoids repeating the definition; on older versions repeat the OVER clause.
questions.tip: Trading days are not calendar days, so I use ROWS here; RANGE with 6 days would silently shrink the window across weekends.
questions.simple: To smooth out a stock's daily ups and downs, you take today's price and the 6 days before it, and find the average. Tomorrow you slide one day forward and do it again. That sliding window of 7 rows is a moving average. Until you have 7 days, there is not enough data, so it stays empty.
questions.remember: Moving average = a 7-day window that slides forward.

questions.title: Balance falling three days running
questions.scenario: Treasury wants to spot corporate accounts whose end-of-day balance fell for 3 or more days in a row, with the start and end date of each fall.
questions.schema:
DAILY_BAL(acct_id NUMBER, bal_date DATE, balance NUMBER(18,2))
-- one row per account per day
questions.task: Return acct_id, start date of the fall, end date, and number of falling days, for each run of 3 or more consecutive daily decreases.
questions.hint: Define a row pattern: a starting row followed by 3 or more rows each lower than the one before.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id, start_dt, end_dt, falling_days
FROM daily_bal
MATCH_RECOGNIZE (
  PARTITION BY acct_id
  ORDER BY bal_date
  MEASURES FIRST(bal_date) AS start_dt,
           LAST(bal_date)  AS end_dt,
           COUNT(down.bal_date) AS falling_days
  ONE ROW PER MATCH
  PATTERN (strt down{3,})
  DEFINE down AS balance < PREV(balance)
);
questions.why: PATTERN works like a regular expression over rows. strt matches any row; down{3,} needs at least 3 following rows, each below its previous row. MEASURES picks what to report per match.
questions.tip: For pattern-over-rows problems MATCH_RECOGNIZE is clearer than nested analytic functions; I can also explain the gaps-and-islands alternative if the team avoids it.
questions.simple: You are looking for a pattern like 'down, down, down' in daily balances, the way you would look for a word in a sentence. MATCH_RECOGNIZE lets you describe the pattern (one start day, then 3 or more falling days) and Oracle finds every place it happens.
questions.remember: MATCH_RECOGNIZE = search for a pattern across rows.

questions.title: First transaction after long silence
questions.scenario: Regulations require extra checks when a dormant account suddenly becomes active. Risk wants every transaction that came more than 2 years after the previous transaction on that account.
questions.schema: TXN(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_date DATE, amount NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: List acct_id, txn_id, txn_date, previous transaction date and the gap in days, where the gap is more than 24 months.
questions.hint: Compare each transaction's date with the previous one for the same account.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id, txn_id, txn_date, prev_date,
       txn_date - prev_date AS gap_days
FROM (
  SELECT t.*,
         LAG(txn_date) OVER (PARTITION BY acct_id
                             ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id) AS prev_date
  FROM txn t
)
WHERE txn_date > ADD_MONTHS(prev_date, 24);
questions.why: LAG brings the previous transaction date onto the current row. ADD_MONTHS handles leap years correctly, which a fixed 730 days would not. First transactions have NULL prev_date and drop out naturally.
questions.tip: I avoid hard-coded day counts for regulatory periods and use ADD_MONTHS so leap years do not create false positives.
questions.simple: Think of a friend who has not texted you for 2 years and suddenly messages. That is unusual, so you check it. Here, for every transaction you look at the date of the previous one on the same account using LAG. If the gap is more than 24 months, you flag it.
questions.remember: LAG to get the last date, then measure the gap.

questions.title: Customers holding 80% of deposits
questions.scenario: Management believes a small set of customers holds most of the deposits. They want the list of customers who, taken from the largest down, make up the first 80% of total deposits.
questions.schema:
CUST_DEPOSIT(cust_id NUMBER, total_deposit NUMBER(18,2))
-- one row per customer
questions.task: Return cust_id, total_deposit and cumulative percentage, for customers up to the point where the cumulative share first reaches 80%.
questions.hint: Running sum divided by grand total. Include the customer who crosses the 80% line.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, total_deposit, ROUND(cum_pct, 2) AS cum_pct
FROM (
  SELECT c.*,
         100 * SUM(total_deposit) OVER (ORDER BY total_deposit DESC, cust_id
                 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
             / SUM(total_deposit) OVER () AS cum_pct
  FROM cust_deposit c
)
WHERE cum_pct - 100 * total_deposit / (SELECT SUM(total_deposit) FROM cust_deposit) < 80;
questions.why: SUM() OVER () is the grand total; the ordered SUM is the running total. The filter keeps a customer when the share before them was still under 80%, so the one who crosses the line is included.
questions.tip: An empty OVER () gives a grand total on every row without a join; that is the cheapest way to compute percent-of-total.
questions.simple: Imagine a class where a few students have most of the marbles. You line them up from the most marbles to the least and keep a running total. You stop when the running total reaches 80% of all marbles. Those students hold most of the deposits.
questions.remember: Sort big to small, keep a running total, stop at 80%.

questions.title: Interest on daily balances
questions.scenario: Savings interest is calculated on the balance held each day. The table stores a row only when the balance changes, so each balance applies until the next change.
questions.schema:
BAL_CHANGE(acct_id NUMBER, eff_date DATE, balance NUMBER(16,2))
-- balance is valid from eff_date until the next row's eff_date
-- quarter: 01-JAN-2026 to 31-MAR-2026 inclusive, rate 3.5% a year, 365-day basis
questions.task: Compute interest per account for the quarter, rounded to 2 decimals. Assume every account has a row on 01-JAN-2026.
questions.hint: LEAD gives the next change date; use the day after quarter end as the default for the last row.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id,
       ROUND(SUM(balance * 3.5 / 100 * days_held / 365), 2) AS interest
FROM (
  SELECT acct_id, balance,
         LEAD(eff_date, 1, DATE '2026-04-01')
           OVER (PARTITION BY acct_id ORDER BY eff_date) - eff_date AS days_held
  FROM bal_change
  WHERE eff_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
    AND eff_date <  DATE '2026-04-01'
)
GROUP BY acct_id;
questions.why: LEAD's third argument is the default when no next row exists, so the last balance runs to the end of the quarter. Rounding once after summing avoids losing paise on every row.
questions.tip: With money I round once at the end, not per row, and I confirm the day-count basis (365 or actual) with the business before coding.
questions.simple: A balance stays the same until it changes, like a light that stays on until someone flips the switch. LEAD tells you when the next change happens, so you know how many days each balance lasted. Then interest = balance × rate × days ÷ 365, and you add it all up.
questions.remember: LEAD = peek at the next row to find when this one ends.

questions.concept: BULK COLLECT and FORALL with SAVE EXCEPTIONS
questions.title: Post quarterly interest in bulk
questions.scenario: The interest posting job handles 2 crore accounts. The current row-by-row loop takes hours, and one bad row aborts the run. It must be fast and must skip and log bad rows.
questions.schema:
INTEREST_DUE(acct_id NUMBER, interest NUMBER(12,2))
ACCT_BALANCE(acct_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, balance NUMBER(16,2))
ERR_LOG(acct_id NUMBER, err_code NUMBER, logged_on DATE)
questions.task: Write a PL/SQL block that reads INTEREST_DUE in batches of 10,000, updates balances with FORALL, logs failed rows to ERR_LOG and carries on.
questions.hint: BULK COLLECT ... LIMIT inside a loop, FORALL ... SAVE EXCEPTIONS, then read SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS.
questions.why: BULK COLLECT and FORALL send rows to the SQL engine in batches, cutting context switches. LIMIT caps memory. SAVE EXCEPTIONS lets the batch finish and raises ORA-24381 once, with the failed positions in SQL%BULK_EXCEPTIONS. Exit on COUNT = 0, not %NOTFOUND, or the last partial batch is lost.
questions.tip: I always use LIMIT with BULK COLLECT, and I exit on collection count, because %NOTFOUND is true on the final partial fetch.
questions.simple: Doing 2 crore updates one by one is like carrying bricks one at a time. BULK COLLECT picks up 10,000 bricks in one trip, and FORALL puts them all down in one go. SAVE EXCEPTIONS means if one brick is broken, you note it down and keep going instead of stopping the whole job.
questions.remember: Fetch in batches, update in batches, log the bad ones and carry on.

questions.concept: Row locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE
questions.title: Safe transfer between two accounts
questions.scenario: Two transfers hitting the same account at the same moment have produced a wrong balance. You are asked to write the transfer procedure so that this cannot happen and so two opposite transfers cannot deadlock.
questions.schema: ACCT_BALANCE(acct_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, balance NUMBER(16,2))
questions.task: Write procedure transfer(p_from, p_to, p_amt) that locks both rows, rejects the transfer if funds are insufficient, and updates both balances. The caller commits.
questions.hint: Lock both rows before reading the balance, and always lock in the same order.
questions.why: FOR UPDATE locks the rows, so the balance you checked cannot change before you update it (no lost update). Locking in acct_id order means two opposite transfers ask for locks in the same sequence, so they wait instead of deadlocking. Leaving COMMIT to the caller keeps the debit and credit in one transaction.
questions.tip: Check-then-update without a lock is a race condition; I lock first, in a fixed order, and keep both legs in one transaction.
questions.simple: Two people try to take money from the same piggy bank at the same moment, and the count goes wrong. FOR UPDATE is like putting your hand on the piggy bank so nobody else can touch it until you finish. Always grabbing the lower account number first stops two people from each holding one bank and waiting for the other forever.
questions.remember: Lock first, check, then update; always lock in the same order.

questions.title: Audit log that survives rollback
questions.scenario: Audit requires every failed transfer attempt to be logged. Today, when the transfer rolls back, the log row is rolled back with it and the evidence is lost.
questions.schema:
AUDIT_LOG(log_id NUMBER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, event VARCHAR2(30),
          details VARCHAR2(400), logged_by VARCHAR2(30), logged_on TIMESTAMP)
questions.task: Write procedure log_event(p_event, p_details) whose insert is committed even when the calling transaction rolls back.
questions.hint: A pragma lets a procedure run in its own independent transaction.
questions.why: PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION starts a separate transaction, so its COMMIT saves only the log row and does not touch the caller's work. It must commit or roll back before returning, otherwise ORA-06519 is raised.
questions.tip: I use autonomous transactions only for logging and auditing; using them to dodge a mutating-table error hides a design problem.
questions.simple: Imagine you tear up a bad homework page, but you still want a note in your diary saying you tried. An autonomous transaction is like a separate diary: you write in it and save it, even if the main work is thrown away.
questions.remember: Autonomous transaction = a separate save that survives rollback.

questions.title: Daily ATM limit without ORA-04091
questions.scenario: A row-level trigger was written to block ATM withdrawals above Rs 50,000 a day per account. It queries the same table it fires on and fails with ORA-04091: table is mutating.
questions.schema: ATM_TXN(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_date DATE, amount NUMBER(10,2))
questions.task: Rewrite it as a compound trigger on INSERT that rejects the statement if any affected account's total for that day goes above 50,000.
questions.hint: Collect the affected accounts in the row section; run the check in AFTER STATEMENT, when the table is no longer mutating.
questions.why: A row-level trigger cannot read the table being changed. A compound trigger shares state between sections: the row section only remembers which account and day were touched, and the statement section, where the table is stable, runs the query. The error rolls back the whole statement.
questions.tip: Mutating table means my row trigger is reading its own table; I move the read to the statement level with a compound trigger rather than hiding it with an autonomous transaction.
questions.simple: A row trigger is not allowed to look at the table while it is still changing it, like trying to count people in a room while they are still walking in. A compound trigger notes down who came in during the row part, and does the counting at the end, when everyone has sat down.
questions.remember: Remember in the row part, check in the statement part.

questions.title: Days-past-due ageing report
questions.scenario: The collections manager wants the overdue loan book split into ageing buckets, showing how many loans and how much money sits in each.
questions.schema:
LOAN_DUE(loan_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, due_date DATE, outstanding_amt NUMBER(14,2))
-- only unpaid dues are in this table
questions.task: As of today, show bucket ('1-30', '31-60', '61-90', '90+'), number of loans and total outstanding. Ignore dues that are not yet overdue. Order from youngest to oldest bucket.
questions.hint: Compute days past due once in an inline view, then bucket with CASE.
questions.solution:
SELECT bucket, COUNT(*) AS loans, SUM(outstanding_amt) AS total_os
FROM (
  SELECT outstanding_amt,
         CASE
           WHEN dpd <= 30 THEN '1-30'
           WHEN dpd <= 60 THEN '31-60'
           WHEN dpd <= 90 THEN '61-90'
           ELSE '90+'
         END AS bucket,
         CASE WHEN dpd <= 30 THEN 1 WHEN dpd <= 60 THEN 2
              WHEN dpd <= 90 THEN 3 ELSE 4 END AS sort_no
  FROM (SELECT outstanding_amt, TRUNC(SYSDATE) - TRUNC(due_date) AS dpd
        FROM loan_due)
  WHERE dpd > 0
)
GROUP BY bucket, sort_no
ORDER BY sort_no;
questions.why: CASE stops at the first true branch, so the conditions can be written as simple upper limits. A separate sort column is needed because '90+' would not sort correctly as text.
questions.tip: I TRUNC both dates so the time part does not push a loan into the wrong bucket around midnight.
questions.simple: Think of sorting late library books into boxes: 1 to 30 days late, 31 to 60, 61 to 90, and more than 90. CASE decides which box each loan goes into. Then you count how many loans are in each box and how much money they owe.
questions.remember: CASE puts each row into a box; GROUP BY counts each box.

questions.title: Customers with no loan
questions.scenario: Marketing wants customers who have never taken a loan. A colleague's query with NOT IN returns zero rows even though such customers clearly exist.
questions.schema:
CUSTOMER(cust_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(60))
LOAN(loan_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, amount NUMBER(14,2))
-- LOAN.cust_id is NULL for a few legacy rows
questions.task: Write the query correctly, and be ready to explain why NOT IN returned nothing.
questions.hint: What does `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` evaluate to?
questions.why: NOT IN expands to cust_id <> a AND cust_id <> b AND cust_id <> NULL. The last comparison is unknown, so the whole condition is never true and no row comes back. NOT EXISTS only tests whether a matching row exists, so NULLs do not matter.
questions.tip: If the subquery column can be NULL, NOT IN silently returns nothing; I use NOT EXISTS by default.
questions.simple: NULL means 'I don't know'. If you ask 'is this customer not 1, not 2, and not unknown?', the answer is 'I don't know', so Oracle returns nobody. NOT EXISTS just asks 'is there any loan for this customer?', and an unknown value does not confuse it.
questions.remember: If NULL can appear, use NOT EXISTS, not NOT IN.

questions.title: All transactions on 31 March
questions.scenario: A year-end report must pick up every transaction dated 31-Mar-2026. The column stores date and time, the table has 40 crore rows, and there is an index on txn_ts.
questions.schema:
TXN(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_ts DATE, amount NUMBER(14,2))
-- index on TXN(txn_ts)
questions.task: Write the filter so that no transaction of that day is missed and the index on txn_ts can be used.
questions.hint: Avoid wrapping the indexed column in a function. Think about 23:59:59.
questions.solution:
SELECT txn_id, acct_id, txn_ts, amount
FROM txn
WHERE txn_ts >= DATE '2026-03-31'
  AND txn_ts <  DATE '2026-04-01';
questions.why: TRUNC(txn_ts) = DATE '2026-03-31' is correct but applies a function to the column, so the normal index cannot be used. BETWEEN 31-Mar and 31-Mar misses everything after midnight. A half-open range (>= start, < next day) is both correct and index-friendly.
questions.tip: I write date filters as half-open ranges on the bare column so the index is usable and the last second of the day is not lost.
questions.simple: A day runs from midnight to just before the next midnight. Instead of saying 'on 31 March', say 'from 31 March 00:00 up to but not including 1 April 00:00'. That catches every second of the day, and Oracle can still use its index, like using the alphabet tabs in a dictionary.
questions.remember: Use >= start and < next day; never wrap the column in a function.

questions.title: Accounts with no activity for 2 years
questions.scenario: Operations must mark accounts as dormant when there has been no customer transaction for 24 months. Accounts that never had a transaction must be included if they were opened more than 24 months ago.
questions.schema:
ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, opened_on DATE, status VARCHAR2(10))
TXN(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_date DATE, amount NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: List acct_id, opened_on and last transaction date for ACTIVE accounts that qualify as dormant today.
questions.hint: An inner join would drop accounts with no transactions at all.
questions.solution:
SELECT a.acct_id, a.opened_on, MAX(t.txn_date) AS last_txn
FROM account a
LEFT JOIN txn t ON t.acct_id = a.acct_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY a.acct_id, a.opened_on
HAVING NVL(MAX(t.txn_date), a.opened_on) < ADD_MONTHS(TRUNC(SYSDATE), -24);
questions.why: LEFT JOIN keeps accounts without transactions; for them MAX(txn_date) is NULL, so NVL falls back to the opening date. The condition goes in HAVING because it uses an aggregate.
questions.tip: Whenever the question says 'including those with none', I reach for an outer join and decide what NULL should mean.
questions.simple: Some accounts never had a single transaction. A normal join would hide them, like a class photo that leaves out absent students. A LEFT JOIN keeps every account. If there is no transaction, use the opening date instead and check if it is older than 2 years.
questions.remember: LEFT JOIN keeps everyone, even those with nothing to match.

questions.title: Active in every month of the quarter
questions.scenario: The relationship team rewards customers who used their debit card in each of the three months of Q4 (January to March 2026).
questions.schema: CARD_TXN(txn_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, txn_date DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2))
questions.task: Return cust_id and total spend for customers with at least one transaction in each of January, February and March 2026.
questions.hint: Count how many different months each customer appears in.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spend
FROM card_txn
WHERE txn_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND txn_date <  DATE '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY cust_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TRUNC(txn_date, 'MM')) = 3;
questions.why: TRUNC(date, 'MM') maps every date to the first of its month. Counting distinct months per customer and requiring 3 means they were present in all three.
questions.tip: For 'in every period' questions I count distinct periods in HAVING instead of joining the table to itself three times.
questions.simple: You want customers who showed up in January, February and March, like a student who attended at least once every month. Turn each date into its month, count how many different months each customer has, and keep those with 3.
questions.remember: Count distinct months; 3 means present every month.

questions.title: Accounts missing from the KYC register
questions.scenario: Before a regulatory submission, compliance needs two lists: active customers who have no KYC record, and KYC records that belong to no active customer.
questions.schema:
CUSTOMER(cust_id NUMBER, status VARCHAR2(10))
KYC(cust_id NUMBER, kyc_status VARCHAR2(10))
questions.task: Return both lists in one result with a column saying which problem each cust_id has.
questions.hint: MINUS gives rows in the first set that are not in the second.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, 'NO KYC RECORD' AS issue
FROM (SELECT cust_id FROM customer WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
      MINUS
      SELECT cust_id FROM kyc)
UNION ALL
SELECT cust_id, 'KYC WITHOUT ACTIVE CUSTOMER'
FROM (SELECT cust_id FROM kyc
      MINUS
      SELECT cust_id FROM customer WHERE status = 'ACTIVE');
questions.why: MINUS removes duplicates and treats NULLs as equal, which makes it handy for comparing key lists. UNION ALL joins the two lists without an unnecessary sort, since they cannot overlap.
questions.tip: I use UNION ALL unless I really need duplicates removed, because UNION adds a sort.
questions.simple: You have two lists of names. MINUS gives the names on the first list that are missing from the second, like checking who did not hand in homework. Do it both ways to catch missing records on either side.
questions.remember: A MINUS B = in A but not in B.

questions.title: Credits, debits and net per account
questions.scenario: The statement summary needs, for each account in March 2026, total credits, total debits, net movement and the number of transactions, all in one row.
questions.schema: TXN(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_date DATE, dr_cr CHAR(2), amount NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: Return acct_id, total_cr, total_dr, net (credits minus debits) and txn_count for March 2026, reading the table once.
questions.hint: Put a CASE inside SUM.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN dr_cr = 'CR' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS total_cr,
       SUM(CASE WHEN dr_cr = 'DR' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS total_dr,
       SUM(CASE WHEN dr_cr = 'CR' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) AS net,
       COUNT(*) AS txn_count
FROM txn
WHERE txn_date >= DATE '2026-03-01'
  AND txn_date <  DATE '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY acct_id;
questions.why: A CASE inside an aggregate lets one scan produce several conditional totals. ELSE 0 keeps the result 0 rather than NULL for accounts with only credits or only debits.
questions.tip: Conditional aggregation replaces several subqueries with one table scan, which is what I look for first when a report is slow.
questions.simple: Think of one walk through your wallet's receipts, where you keep two piles: money in and money out. A CASE inside SUM lets you add to the right pile as you go, so one pass gives credits, debits and the net.
questions.remember: SUM(CASE ...) = many totals in one pass.

questions.title: Find reversed transactions
questions.scenario: Operations wants to see transactions that were reversed the same day: a debit and a credit on the same account for the same amount on the same date.
questions.schema: TXN(txn_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, txn_date DATE, dr_cr CHAR(2), amount NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: List each debit with its matching credit: acct_id, date, amount, debit txn_id and credit txn_id. The credit must have been posted after the debit.
questions.hint: Join the table to itself: one alias for debits, one for credits.
questions.solution:
SELECT d.acct_id, TRUNC(d.txn_date) AS txn_day, d.amount,
       d.txn_id AS debit_id, c.txn_id AS credit_id
FROM txn d
JOIN txn c
  ON  c.acct_id = d.acct_id
  AND c.amount  = d.amount
  AND TRUNC(c.txn_date) = TRUNC(d.txn_date)
  AND c.txn_id  > d.txn_id
WHERE d.dr_cr = 'DR'
  AND c.dr_cr = 'CR';
questions.why: Two aliases let you compare rows of the same table. The txn_id condition enforces order and stops a row pairing with itself. If the same amount is debited twice, this pairs each debit with each later credit, which you should mention.
questions.tip: With self-joins I always state how I prevent duplicate pairs and what happens when several rows match.
questions.simple: To find a payment and its refund, you compare the list with itself: one copy for the money going out and one copy for the money coming back. You match the same account, amount and day, and make sure the refund came after the payment.
questions.remember: Self-join = compare a table with a copy of itself.

questions.title: Mark loans as NPA
questions.scenario: At month-end, any standard loan with an instalment overdue by more than 90 days must be reclassified as NPA.
questions.schema:
LOAN(loan_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY, status VARCHAR2(10), status_date DATE)
LOAN_DUE(loan_id NUMBER, due_date DATE, paid_flag CHAR(1))
questions.task: Write one UPDATE that sets status to 'NPA' and status_date to today for loans currently 'STANDARD' that have at least one unpaid due older than 90 days.
questions.hint: EXISTS with a correlated subquery.
questions.solution:
UPDATE loan l
   SET l.status = 'NPA',
       l.status_date = TRUNC(SYSDATE)
 WHERE l.status = 'STANDARD'
   AND EXISTS (
         SELECT 1
         FROM loan_due d
         WHERE d.loan_id = l.loan_id
           AND d.paid_flag = 'N'
           AND d.due_date < TRUNC(SYSDATE) - 90
       );
questions.why: EXISTS stops at the first qualifying due, so a loan with ten overdue instalments is still updated once. Filtering on status = 'STANDARD' keeps the statement safe to re-run.
questions.tip: I write batch updates so they can be re-run safely: the WHERE clause excludes rows already processed.
questions.simple: You go through the loan list and ask, for each loan, 'is there any payment more than 90 days overdue?' If yes, mark it NPA. EXISTS stops looking as soon as it finds one, so it is quick.
questions.remember: EXISTS = 'is there at least one?'

questions.title: EMI overdue days and penalty
questions.scenario: Customer service needs a list of customers with overdue EMIs, how many days late each one is, and the penalty at Rs 50 per day capped at Rs 2,000.
questions.schema:
CUSTOMER(cust_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(60), mobile VARCHAR2(15))
LOAN(loan_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER)
EMI(loan_id NUMBER, due_date DATE, emi_amt NUMBER(12,2), paid_on DATE)
-- paid_on is NULL when unpaid
questions.task: Show cust_name, mobile, loan_id, due_date, days_late and penalty for every unpaid EMI that is past its due date, latest first by days late.
questions.hint: LEAST() applies the cap.
questions.solution:
SELECT c.cust_name, c.mobile, l.loan_id, e.due_date,
       TRUNC(SYSDATE) - e.due_date AS days_late,
       LEAST((TRUNC(SYSDATE) - e.due_date) * 50, 2000) AS penalty
FROM emi e
JOIN loan l     ON l.loan_id = e.loan_id
JOIN customer c ON c.cust_id = l.cust_id
WHERE e.paid_on IS NULL
  AND e.due_date < TRUNC(SYSDATE)
ORDER BY days_late DESC;
questions.why: Subtracting two DATEs gives days. LEAST returns the smaller of the computed penalty and the cap. Unpaid is tested with IS NULL, since = NULL is never true.
questions.tip: I check NULL with IS NULL and truncate SYSDATE so the time of day does not add a partial day.
questions.simple: Subtracting two dates gives the number of days in between, like counting days on a calendar. Multiply the days late by 50 rupees, and LEAST makes sure the fine never goes above 2,000.
questions.remember: Date minus date = days; LEAST puts a ceiling on a number.

questions.title: Accounts in each branch
questions.scenario: Ramesh, a regional manager, wants to know how many accounts each branch has, so he can plan staff.
questions.schema: ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, branch_id NUMBER, acct_type VARCHAR2(10), balance NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: Show branch_id and the number of accounts in that branch.
questions.hint: Group the rows by branch, then count each group.
questions.solution:
SELECT branch_id, COUNT(*) AS accounts
FROM account
GROUP BY branch_id
ORDER BY branch_id;
questions.simple: Imagine sorting coins into piles by colour, then counting each pile. GROUP BY makes one pile per branch, and COUNT(*) counts the accounts in each pile.
questions.remember: GROUP BY makes piles; COUNT counts each pile.
questions.why: GROUP BY collapses all rows with the same branch_id into one result row, and COUNT(*) counts how many rows went into it. Every column in SELECT must be either grouped or inside an aggregate.
questions.tip: Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT must also be in the GROUP BY.

questions.title: Five biggest balances
questions.scenario: Kavita from wealth management wants to call the 5 customers with the highest balances this week.
questions.schema: ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(60), balance NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: Show the 5 accounts with the highest balance, biggest first.
questions.hint: Sort from biggest to smallest, then take only the first 5 rows.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id, cust_name, balance
FROM account
ORDER BY balance DESC
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;
questions.simple: It is like lining up students from tallest to shortest and picking the first five. ORDER BY balance DESC lines up the accounts from biggest to smallest, and FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY picks the first five.
questions.remember: Sort first, then take the top rows.
questions.why: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY (Oracle 12c and later) is applied after ORDER BY. The older ROWNUM <= 5 is applied before ORDER BY unless you sort inside a subquery, which is a common mistake.
questions.tip: On 12c and later I use FETCH FIRST; with ROWNUM I sort in an inner query first.

questions.title: Customer name next to each account
questions.scenario: The call centre screen shows only account numbers. Deepak wants the customer's name next to each account.
questions.schema:
CUSTOMER(cust_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(60), city VARCHAR2(30))
ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, balance NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: Show acct_id, cust_name and balance for every account.
questions.hint: Match the two tables on cust_id.
questions.simple: Think of two lists: one with roll numbers and marks, one with roll numbers and names. You match them on roll number to see each name with its marks. JOIN does that matching using cust_id.
questions.remember: JOIN matches rows from two tables on a common column.
questions.why: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so Arjun (no account) does not appear. Table aliases (a, c) keep the query short and make it clear which table each column comes from.
questions.tip: Inner join keeps only matches; if I need rows without a match I switch to a LEFT JOIN.

questions.title: Label accounts by balance
questions.scenario: Sunita in marketing wants each account tagged as Premium, Regular or Low so she can send different offers.
questions.schema: ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(60), balance NUMBER(14,2))
questions.task: Show acct_id, cust_name, balance and a tag: 'Premium' for 1,00,000 or more, 'Regular' for 10,000 to 99,999.99, 'Low' below 10,000.
questions.hint: CASE checks conditions from top to bottom and stops at the first true one.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id, cust_name, balance,
       CASE
         WHEN balance >= 100000 THEN 'Premium'
         WHEN balance >= 10000  THEN 'Regular'
         ELSE 'Low'
       END AS tag
FROM account;
questions.simple: CASE is like a sorting hat. It looks at each account's balance and asks: is it 1 lakh or more? Then Premium. If not, is it 10,000 or more? Then Regular. Otherwise Low.
questions.remember: CASE = if this, then that, checked top to bottom.
questions.why: CASE returns the result of the first WHEN that is true, so later conditions only need the lower limit. ELSE catches everything left, including NULL balances.
questions.tip: I order CASE conditions from the strictest to the loosest so each one only needs one limit.

questions.title: Show 'Not added' for missing nominee
questions.scenario: Many old accounts have no nominee. Farah wants a list where an empty nominee shows as 'Not added' instead of a blank.
questions.schema: ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(60), nominee VARCHAR2(60))
questions.task: Show acct_id, cust_name and nominee, with 'Not added' where nominee is missing.
questions.hint: NVL(column, replacement) gives the replacement when the column is NULL.
questions.solution:
SELECT acct_id, cust_name, NVL(nominee, 'Not added') AS nominee
FROM account;
questions.simple: NULL means the box is empty. NVL says: if the box is empty, write 'Not added' in it. If the box has a name, keep the name.
questions.remember: NVL fills an empty box with a default.
questions.why: NVL(a, b) returns b only when a is NULL. Both arguments should be the same data type; COALESCE does the same job and accepts more than two values.
questions.tip: For a default value I use NVL or COALESCE; COALESCE is standard SQL and takes several fallbacks.

questions.title: Only UPI and IMPS payments
questions.scenario: Vikram from the digital team wants to see only instant payments (UPI and IMPS) above Rs 1,000.
questions.schema: PAYMENT(pay_id NUMBER, channel VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(12,2), pay_date DATE)
questions.task: List pay_id, channel and amount for UPI or IMPS payments where amount is more than 1,000.
questions.hint: IN lets you list several allowed values in one condition.
questions.solution:
SELECT pay_id, channel, amount
FROM payment
WHERE channel IN ('UPI', 'IMPS')
  AND amount > 1000;
questions.simple: It is like a guest list at a party: only names on the list get in. IN ('UPI','IMPS') is the guest list for channel, and amount > 1000 is a second check at the door.
questions.remember: IN = is the value on this list?
questions.why: channel IN ('UPI','IMPS') is short for channel = 'UPI' OR channel = 'IMPS'. Writing it with IN avoids the classic bug of mixing OR and AND without brackets.
questions.tip: If I use OR together with AND, I add brackets; IN avoids that trap for lists of values.

questions.title: Customers with more than 2 accounts
questions.scenario: Anjali in relationship banking wants customers who hold more than 2 accounts, to offer them a family banking pack.
questions.schema: ACCOUNT(acct_id NUMBER, cust_id NUMBER, acct_type VARCHAR2(10))
questions.task: Show cust_id and number of accounts for customers with more than 2 accounts.
questions.hint: WHERE filters rows before grouping; you need a filter after grouping.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, COUNT(*) AS accounts
FROM account
GROUP BY cust_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
questions.simple: First you make one pile of accounts per customer and count each pile. Then you keep only the piles with more than 2. WHERE works before piles are made; HAVING works after.
questions.remember: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.
questions.why: WHERE cannot use COUNT(*) because the groups do not exist yet when WHERE runs. HAVING runs after GROUP BY, so it can test aggregates.
questions.tip: WHERE runs before grouping and HAVING after, so conditions on COUNT or SUM go in HAVING.

questions.concept: SUM with GROUP BY on dates
questions.title: Total deposits per day
questions.scenario: Branch manager Shweta wants the total deposits received on each day of the first week of March.
questions.schema:
DEPOSIT(dep_id NUMBER, acct_id NUMBER, dep_date DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- dep_date has no time part
questions.task: Show dep_date and total amount for each day from 1 to 7 March 2026, in date order.
questions.hint: Filter the dates first, then group by date and add up.
questions.solution:
SELECT dep_date, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM deposit
WHERE dep_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-03-01' AND DATE '2026-03-07'
GROUP BY dep_date
ORDER BY dep_date;
questions.simple: Imagine one envelope for each day. You drop every deposit into its day's envelope, then add up the money in each envelope. GROUP BY dep_date makes the envelopes and SUM adds them.
questions.remember: SUM adds up each group.
questions.why: BETWEEN includes both ends, which is safe here because dep_date has no time part. If it had a time, I would use >= 1 March and < 8 March instead.
questions.tip: BETWEEN on dates is only safe when there is no time part; otherwise I use a half-open range.

lessons.why: Running balances and velocity checks give wrong numbers if you pick the wrong frame.
lessons.explain: A window frame decides which rows an analytic function sees. ROWS counts physical rows. RANGE works on the ORDER BY value, so rows with the same value are treated as one group. If you write ORDER BY without a frame, Oracle uses RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, which makes tied rows share one running total.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT 1 id, DATE '2026-03-01' d, 100 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 2, DATE '2026-03-01', 50 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 3, DATE '2026-03-02', 25 FROM dual
)
SELECT id, d, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS range_default,
       SUM(amt) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_frame
FROM t;
-- range_default: 150, 150, 175   rows_frame: 100, 150, 175
lessons.gotcha: Relying on the default frame when the ORDER BY column has duplicates.
lessons.line: I state the frame explicitly and add a tiebreaker column, so running totals are deterministic.
lessons.simple: ROWS counts lines one by one. RANGE groups together lines that have the same value. If two transactions happen on the same day and you use RANGE, they both get the same running total, like two students sharing one roll number. Say ROWS when you mean 'line by line'.
lessons.remember: ROWS = line by line. RANGE = same value, same group.

lessons.why: Bank transaction tables hold years of data; month-end jobs must touch only the month they need.
lessons.explain: A range-partitioned table stores each period in its own segment. If the WHERE clause filters on the partition key without wrapping it in a function, Oracle reads only the matching partitions. You can confirm it in the plan through the Pstart and Pstop columns.
lessons.gotcha: TO_CHAR(txn_date, 'YYYYMM') = '202603' hides the key from the optimizer and scans every partition.
lessons.line: I filter on the bare partition key with a date range and check Pstart and Pstop in the plan to prove pruning happened.
lessons.simple: A big table split by month is like a cupboard with one drawer per month. If you ask for March using plain dates, Oracle opens only the March drawer. If you change the date into text first, Oracle cannot tell which drawer to open and searches all of them.
lessons.remember: Filter on the plain date so Oracle opens only the right drawer.

lessons.why: Payment queues are processed by several workers at once; no payment may be picked twice.
lessons.explain: FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows until commit. With SKIP LOCKED, a session ignores rows already locked by others instead of waiting, so parallel workers each take a different set of pending rows without blocking.
lessons.gotcha: Using ROWNUM = 1 with SKIP LOCKED: ROWNUM is applied before locking, so every worker may target the same row and get nothing.
lessons.line: For queue tables I fetch from a FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED cursor so workers never block or double-process.
lessons.simple: Many workers pick jobs from one pile. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED means: if someone already has their hand on a job, skip it and take the next free one. Nobody waits, and no job is done twice.
lessons.remember: SKIP LOCKED = skip what others are holding.

lessons.why: Wrong totals in a regulatory report often trace back to NULL handling.
lessons.explain: Any comparison with NULL is unknown, so it is never true. Aggregates such as SUM and AVG skip NULLs; COUNT(col) skips them but COUNT(*) does not. AVG therefore divides by the number of non-null values, which may not be what the business expects.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT 100 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 200 FROM dual
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(amt) AS non_null,
       AVG(amt) AS avg_skip_null, AVG(NVL(amt, 0)) AS avg_null_as_zero
FROM t;
-- 3, 2, 150, 100
lessons.gotcha: Writing WHERE col <> 'X' and expecting NULL rows to be included; they are not.
lessons.line: I ask what NULL means for each column before aggregating, and I say which rows my filter leaves out.
lessons.simple: NULL means 'unknown', not zero. Asking 'is unknown equal to 5?' gets the answer 'unknown', so the row is left out. Averages also skip unknowns, so the average of 100, unknown and 200 is 150, not 100.

lessons.why: Month-end queries on large tables must finish inside the batch window.
lessons.explain: EXPLAIN PLAN shows how Oracle intends to run a query. Read it from the most indented line outward. Look at the access path (full scan or index), the join method (nested loops for few rows, hash join for many) and the estimated rows. A large gap between estimated and actual rows usually means stale statistics.
lessons.gotcha: Treating cost as time, or adding hints before checking statistics and predicates.
lessons.line: I compare estimated and actual rows first; if they differ a lot, I fix statistics or the predicate before considering hints.
lessons.simple: An execution plan is Oracle's route map for your query, like Google Maps showing which roads it will take. Read it from the most indented line outwards. Check whether it reads the whole table or uses an index, and whether its guess of row counts is close to reality.
lessons.remember: Plan = Oracle's route map; check how it reads and how many rows it expects.

lessons.why: A batch that swallows errors can post half a file and report success.
lessons.explain: Handle only the errors you can do something about, and let the rest propagate. WHEN OTHERS without RAISE hides failures. Use RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR (-20000 to -20999) for business errors and DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_BACKTRACE to capture the failing line.
lessons.gotcha: WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL: the job looks successful while data is missing.
lessons.line: My rule is log, roll back, re-raise; a handler that hides an error is worse than no handler.
lessons.simple: If something goes wrong, do not hide it. A WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL is like sweeping broken glass under the carpet: everything looks fine but it is not. Note the error, undo the half-done work, and raise the error again so someone knows.
lessons.remember: Log it, roll back, raise it again.

lessons.why: Dashboards and regulatory extracts should not re-aggregate crores of rows on every request.
lessons.explain: A materialized view stores the result of a query. It can be refreshed completely, or incrementally (FAST) using materialized view logs on the base tables. With query rewrite enabled, Oracle can answer matching queries from the stored result automatically.
lessons.example:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_branch_daily
BUILD IMMEDIATE
REFRESH COMPLETE ON DEMAND
AS
SELECT branch_id, TRUNC(txn_date) AS txn_day,
       COUNT(*) AS txn_cnt, SUM(amount) AS total_amt
FROM txn
GROUP BY branch_id, TRUNC(txn_date);

-- refresh after the end-of-day load
EXEC DBMS_MVIEW.REFRESH('MV_BRANCH_DAILY', 'C');
lessons.gotcha: Forgetting that the data is only as fresh as the last refresh; reports must show the refresh time.
lessons.line: I use materialized views for heavy aggregates read often and changed in batches, and I tie the refresh to the end of the load job.
lessons.simple: A materialized view is a saved answer, like writing the result of a long sum on a sticky note so you do not redo it every time. It is fast to read, but you must refresh the note when the numbers change.
lessons.remember: Saved answer: fast to read, refresh it after loads.

lessons.why: Bulk processing in banking batches depends on picking the right collection type.
lessons.explain: Associative arrays (INDEX BY) live only in PL/SQL memory and are good for lookups by key. Nested tables can be used with BULK COLLECT, in SQL through TABLE(), and stored in columns. VARRAYs have a fixed maximum size. Nested tables and VARRAYs must be initialised; associative arrays need not be.
lessons.gotcha: Looping 1..COUNT over a sparse collection after deletes raises NO_DATA_FOUND; use FIRST and NEXT.
lessons.line: Associative array for in-memory lookup, nested table for bulk SQL work; I choose by where the data has to go.
lessons.simple: Collections are boxes to hold many values in PL/SQL. An associative array is like a dictionary: you look up a value by its name. A nested table is like a numbered list you can send to SQL in bulk.
lessons.remember: Look up by key: associative array. Bulk to SQL: nested table.
